SOURCE: "Graph Neural Prompting with Large Language Models", Yijun Tian, Huan Song, Zichen Wang, Haozhu Wang, Ziqing Hu, Fang Wang, Nitesh V. Chawla, Panpan Xu (Notre Dame, Amazon). arXiv:2309.15427v2 (28 Dec 2023). The page-1 copyright line is AAAI 2024 ("Copyright © 2024, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence"). The extraction does not print the venue name otherwise. Title and arXiv ID match what you expected.

COVERAGE: All 9 of 9 pages. I read about 40,000 of 45,930 chars in full. The last ~6k chars are the reference list, which I did not read past "Mihaylov... Can a". The paper has no appendix and no limitations section. The extraction was clean, with only garbled math symbols (eq. 7).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Frozen LLM: GNP beats every baseline, including Prompt Tuning, with +12.76% (3B) and +13.54% (11B) on the six-dataset average.
  number: 74.36 vs 65.95 (3B); 77.84 vs 68.55 (11B)
  setup: FLAN-T5 xlarge (3B) and xxlarge (11B), LLM frozen, only the graph prompt trained. Accuracy on OBQA, ARC, PIQA, RiddleSense, PubMedQA and BioASQ, with the "Total" column as the average. The KGs are ConceptNet and UMLS.
  quote: "In general, GNP achieves an improvement of+12.76% and +13.54% for 3B and 11B LLM, respectively."
  where: p.5, Table 1 and Performance Comparison text
- Putting KG triples into the prompt as text (KG Flattening, KAPING) hurts the frozen LLM, and often scores below the no-KG baseline.
  number: 11B totals: LLM-only 66.88, KG Flattening REL 64.35, BFS 64.20, KAPING TH 59.15, KAPING OH 58.87. 3B totals: LLM-only 64.49, REL 60.18, BFS 60.29, KAPING TH 58.41, KAPING OH 58.53. On 11B OBQA, LLM-only scores 76.80 and KAPING scores 60.00-60.60.
  setup: same as above. Baselines are KG Flattening (REL = relevance-score ranking, BFS) and KAPING (one-hop and two-hop triples, Baek et al. 2023). Triples are fed in as hard text.
  quote: "Interestingly, the baseline methods that inject KG information directly (KG Flattening and KAPING) can significantly hurt the model performance. This aligns with our motivation that KGs contain irrelevant contexts for the downstream tasks that could introduce noises or even alter the semantics if not handled carefully."
  where: p.5
- The gains are largest on the hardest or most KG-aligned sets, and small on PIQA and ARC.
  number: BioASQ +34.14% (3B) and +38.75% (11B) over Prompt Tuning. RiddleSense +25.37% (3B) and +15.66% (11B). PIQA +1.07% (3B) and +3.92% (11B). ARC +1.71% (3B) and +4.48% (11B).
  setup: frozen LLM, Δ is relative to Prompt Tuning. BioASQ goes 66.67 to 89.43 (3B) and 65.04 to 90.24 (11B).
  quote: "GNP provides +25.37% improvement on Riddle for 3B LLM, and +15.66% improvement for 11B LLM. In addition, for the biomedical reasoning task, GNP improves the performance by +34.14% on BioASQ for 3B LLM and +38.75% for 11B LLM."
  where: p.5
- Abstract/Fig. 1 headline: +13.5% with the LLM frozen and +1.8% over LoRA when tuned.
  number: +13.5% frozen, +1.8% with LoRA. LoRA + GNP totals are 77.43 (3B) and 80.83 (11B), against LoRA alone at 76.23 and 79.41.
  setup: averaged over six datasets for the 11B model (Fig. 1). The per-dataset LoRA gains range from 0.00% to 3.73%. On PubMedQA and BioASQ at 3B the gain is 0.00%.
  quote: "GNP improves the baseline by +13.5% when LLM is frozen, validating the superiority of our method in learning effective prompts. In addition, by using our method, fine-tuning LLMs with parameter-efficient approach LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) shows an improvement of +1.8%."
  where: p.1-2
- LoRA + GNP matches or beats full fine-tuning in 10 of 12 evaluations.
  number: 10 of 12. Full fine-tuning totals are 76.85 (3B) and 80.55 (11B). LoRA+GNP totals are 77.43 and 80.83.
  setup: 2 LLM sizes x 6 datasets. Full fine-tuning is shown only as a reference. The tuning gains are small, and the 12 are not independent runs.
  quote: "our final performance matches or surpasses model full fine-tuning in 10 out of 12 evaluations across different LLM sizes and datasets"
  where: p.5
- Frozen GNP nearly closes the gap to LoRA at 3B on some sets, but not on all.
  number: frozen GNP total is 74.36 (3B) and 77.84 (11B). LoRA is 76.23 and 79.41. Full fine-tuning is 76.85 and 80.55.
  setup: derived from Table 1, so it is my reading and not a claim the authors make.
  quote: "GNP 79.80 71.85 61.48 66.86 76.75 89.43 74.36"
  where: p.4, Table 1
- Ablation: the domain projector matters most, and removing any component hurts.
  number: 3B OBQA goes 79.80 to 73.00 without the domain projector (DP). 11B PubMedQA goes 76.25 to 71.75 without DP. 11B BioASQ goes 90.24 to 85.37 without DP.
  setup: Table 2, four datasets (OBQA, ARC, PubMedQA, BioASQ). Components are CMP (cross-modality pooling), SLP (self-supervised link prediction) and DP.
  quote: "removing DP significantly affects the performance, showing that DP has a large contribution to the proposed method."
  where: p.5, Table 2
- Instance-level prompts from the retrieved subgraph are enough. Adding a dataset-level prompt (DLP) does not help, and a relational GNN (RGNN) does not beat a plain GAT.
  number: 11B ARC goes 78.20 to 76.05 with DLP and to 76.48 with RGNN. 11B OBQA goes 87.20 to 86.20 with DLP and to 85.20 with RGNN.
  setup: Table 3.
  quote: "a standard GNN is sufficient to capture the graph information, and explicitly modeling the relations might increase the difficulty of generating suitable guidance for the task."
  where: p.5
- The best number of GNN layers and pooling layers varies by dataset and model size, so it must be tuned per dataset.
  number: 11B ARC falls from 78.1 to 74.3 going from 3 to 5 GNN layers.
  setup: layers are searched over 2-5 for the GNN and 1-3 for pooling.
  quote: "increasing from 3 layers to 5 layers for 11B LLM can decrease the performance on ARC by a large margin (from 78.1 to 74.3)"
  where: p.5-6

METHOD (for the note)
- Pipeline:
  1. Entity-link the question and options to a KG.
  2. Retrieve the 2-hop subgraph.
  3. Encode it with a GAT, initialised from pre-trained entity embeddings.
  4. Apply self-attention, then cross-attention with the node embeddings as query and the LLM token embeddings as key and value (cross-modality pooling).
  5. Average-pool to one vector.
  6. Run an MLP "domain projector" to the LLM embedding dimension, giving a single soft "Graph Neural Prompt" prepended to the input embeddings.
  7. Train with the LLM loss plus a DistMult link-prediction loss on masked edges, L = Lllm + λLlp.
- Only the GNN, pooling and projector are trained when the LLM is frozen. The authors call it plug-and-play.
- Task: multiple-choice QA, with the subgraph retrieved per answer option.
- Hyperparameters: lr 1e-4, batch 8, GNN hidden 1024, 50 epochs, λ in {0.1, 0.5}, link drop rate in {0.1, 0.3, 0.7}, 4x V100 24GB.
- quote: "GNP retrieves and encodes the pertinent grounded knowledge to derive Graph Neural Prompt, an embedding vector that can be sent into LLMs to provide guidance and instructions."

LIMITS
- Models are only FLAN-T5 3B and 11B, which are encoder-decoder and open-weight. Nothing is shown on decoder-only chat LLMs or API models, because soft prompts need access to the input embeddings.
- Tasks are multiple-choice QA only. There is no free-form generation, no multi-hop question answering over a custom KG, and no text-to-Cypher or text-to-query.
- The KGs are fixed public ones (ConceptNet, UMLS). Retrieval is plain entity linking plus a 2-hop expansion, and it is not evaluated on its own. It is not a graph-database query pipeline.
- The method needs training for each dataset, with a per-dataset search over layers and hyperparameters. The authors do not report cost, latency or variance, and there are no seeds or confidence intervals.
- The paper has no limitations section. The authors concede only that the KG can contain irrelevant entities: the case study shows noise such as "round" and "nursery".
- The KAPING and KG Flattening baselines are reimplemented as zero-shot hard-text prompts into a frozen FLAN-T5. They are not tuned.
- The "Prompt Designs*" row reports only the best of several prompts. The authors do not define the evaluation split sizes in the text.
- The case study uses two hand-picked OBQA examples (Fig. 5), which is anecdotal.
- Dated: 2023, and from the same era as KAPING and DRAGON. It predates GraphRAG-style summarisation and LLM-driven Cypher generation.

BUILDS ON
- KAPING (Baek, Aji, Saffari 2023), as a baseline.
- DRAGON (Yasunaga et al. 2022) for the 2-hop subgraph retrieval and the REL ranking.
- QAGNN (Yasunaga et al. 2021) and GreaseLM (Zhang et al. 2022) for KG-augmented question answering. GreaseLM also supplies the RGNN.
- MHGRN (Feng et al. 2020) for the pre-trained entity embeddings.
- GAT (Velickovic et al. 2018) for the encoder.
- DistMult (Yang et al. 2015) for link prediction.
- Prompt Tuning (Lester, Al-Rfou, Constant 2021) and Prefix-tuning (Li and Liang 2021) for soft prompts.
- LoRA (Hu et al. 2022).
- RAG (Lewis et al. 2020), cited for the motivation.
- FLAN-T5 (Chung et al. 2022).
- Datasets and KGs: OBQA, ARC, PIQA, RiddleSense, PubMedQA, BioASQ, ConceptNet (Speer et al. 2017), UMLS (Bodenreider 2004).

CODE: none in the paper. The authors link https://github.com/meettyj/GNP. Key equations, for reference:
- (4) H3 = softmax[H2 · (T′)^T / sqrt(dg)] · T′
- (6) Z = FFN3(σ(FFN4(H4)))
- (8) L = Lllm + λLlp

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p.1): bar comparison of Frozen vs Tuned averaged over six datasets for 11B. It is the quickest view of the +13.5% and +1.8% headline.
- Fig. 2 (p.2-3): overall framework. It shows retrieve subgraph -> GNN -> cross-modality pooling -> projector -> soft prompt -> LLM, with the link-prediction side loss.
- Fig. 3 and 4 (p.5-6): sensitivity to GNN layers and pooling layers.
- Fig. 5 (p.6): case study of retrieved OBQA subgraphs, which shows the noisy entities. I did not run the figure-caption script, and I have only the captions from the extracted text.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The only extraction faults are the garbled math symbols, and the Table 1 gray-colour marking of the full-fine-tuning rows is lost. For the note, treat this as a soft-prompt method for frozen or tuned FLAN-T5. It is not text-to-Cypher or graph-database RAG. Its relevance to the note is the evidence that putting raw triples into the prompt can hurt, and that a learned encoding of the subgraph helps.
